title: In Your 40s, Gaining Weight Even Though You Eat the Same: What Changes and What to Do
intro: You're not imagining it, many women in their 40s really do find weight goes up more easily even though they eat the same. The good news is, many of the main reasons can be changed with small, consistent steps.

sections.p: With age, muscle usually decreases bit by bit if you don't train it. We also sit more, move less and our sleep may be disturbed. For some women, hormone changes around perimenopause can also have an effect. If you're worried about your hormones or thyroid, it's good to see a doctor for a check.

Strength training helps maintain muscle, and muscle helps your body use energy better. Start with 2 sessions a week, 20-30 minutes is enough. Squats to a chair, wall push-ups and lifting water bottles are already a start.
Make sure every meal has a protein source. For example, eggs in the morning, chicken or fish at lunch, tofu or tempeh at night. Protein helps you stay full longer and supports your muscles.

sections.h: A little less rice, not none
sections.p: One cup of cooked white rice is an estimated 200 kcal. If you usually take two scoops, try one and a half first. Fill the empty space with vegetables. Small changes like this are easy to keep up.
Lack of sleep and work stress can increase your appetite, especially for sweet foods. Try to set a more consistent bedtime. Cut down on screens 30 minutes before bed.

action: Do 2 light strength training sessions at home this week, 20 minutes each.
Add one protein source to breakfast, for example a hard-boiled egg or an omelette.
Cut your rice by half a scoop at lunch and add vegetables.
Walk for 10 minutes after dinner on at least 3 days.
Note down your bedtime for a week to see the pattern.
myth: Many people believe metabolism drops suddenly once you turn 40. Actually, the big changes usually come from losing muscle and moving less, and both of these can be improved.

faq.q: Does perimenopause really make it hard to lose weight?
faq.a: For some women, hormone changes can affect sleep, appetite and fat storage. Everyone is different, so talk to your doctor if you have symptoms that bother you. Eating habits, lifting weights and sleep still help.

faq.q: Do I need to eat very little to lose weight?
faq.a: No need, and it's not recommended. Eating too little can make you lose muscle and get tired quickly. A small, consistent deficit is safer and easier to maintain.

faq.q: How fast should my weight go down?
faq.a: A realistic target is around 0.5 to 1 kg a week, and sometimes slower. Also pay attention to your waist measurement and body strength, not just the scale.
